chunks: What sets slew rate and rise time. The question: What determines slew rate and rise/fall time?
Slew rate and rise time are two different speed limits. Slew rate is the largest rate the output can change, set by how much current is available to charge a capacitor.
Rise time is how long a small, well-behaved step takes, set by bandwidth. Which one limits you depends on the size of the step.
Picture filling a bathtub through a valve that opens smoothly. For a small top-up, the level eases in at a pace set by how quickly the valve responds.
For a big fill, the valve is wide open and you are limited by the most water the pipe can carry per second, so the level climbs in a straight line.
The valve's response is the bandwidth limit, and the pipe's maximum flow is the slew limit.
The compensation capacitor connects the output of the second stage back to the high-impedance node between the stages.
The first stage must supply (or sink) the current that charges C c .
Slew rate: the maximum rate of change of the output, in volts per microsecond (V/µs; a microsecond is a millionth of a second).
Rise time: the time for the output to go from 10% to 90% of a step. Bandwidth: roughly the highest frequency the amplifier handles well (its minus 3 decibels point).
It sets the rise time of small signals. Tail current ( I tail ): the fixed current the op-amp's first (input) stage runs on.
Compensation capacitor ( C c ): the capacitor inside the op-amp that the current charges.
Say an op-amp has 10 microamps of tail current and a 20 picofarads compensation capacitor. The slew rate is I over C equals 10 microamps over 20 picofarads equals 0.
5 volts per microsecond. A big 10 volts step then ramps in a straight line for 10 over 0. 5 equals 20 microseconds. Its rise time, the middle 8 volts from 10% to 90%, is 8 over 0.
5 equals 16 microseconds, however much bandwidth the part has. A tiny step stays under the slew limit, so only the bandwidth sets how fast it moves. That is the whole idea.
